 Rangers’ top line starting to click — even with glaring weakness to turnaround 
 By 
 Andrew Crane 
 Published 
 Nov. 16, 2026, 8:34 p.m. ET 
 See more of our coverage in your search results. 
 Make New York Post a Preferred Source 
 Maybe the West Coast trip was a turning point, a four-game window where everything started to come together for the Rangers top line of Mika Zibanejad, Alexis Lafrenière and Gabe Perreault and then stayed that way. Maybe a moment like Friday — when the trio combined for a nifty tic-tac-toe goal off the rush against the Canucks — becomes repeatable.

 From the first day of training camp, the Blueshirts wanted to find a way to recapture the chemistry of that line, which emerged as their most productive one down the stretch last year as the breakthroughs of Lafrenière and Perreault combined with the consistency of Zibanejad. At times, they’ve struggled to replicate that cohesion. The analytics show they give up as many chances as they produce at times, a variable limiting their overarching potential within the Mike Sullivan system. But across four games in Seattle and Western Canada, when they combined for five goals — with four while all on the ice at 5-on-5 — and 10 assists, they might’ve discovered a blueprint for the offensive side of their game. 
 “The longer you play together, too, you’re bound to have moments and times during the season where you might not feel at the top of your game in terms of as a line and be connected,” Zibanejad said before the Rangers hosted the Canadiens at the Garden on Monday. “We know what we’re capable of doing off the rush and the plays that we can make.” 
 The Zibanejad-Lafrenière-Perreault line entered play Monday ranked 22nd in the NHL in expected goals per 60 minutes among lines with at least 100 minutes together in 2026-27, according to MoneyPuck, and they have the 12th-best expected goals against per 60 minutes (2.26). But in three of the four West Coast games, the line had an expected goals for percentage lower than 52, according to Natural Stat Trick — the worst number among the Blueshirts lines in those matches and a tangible sign of being nearly outplayed when on the ice instead of controlling play. Part of that, to some degree, becomes inevitable when skating against an opponent’s top six, though. 
 New York Rangers’ Alexis Lafreniere (13) celebrates his goal with Gabe Perreault (94) and Mika Zibanejad (93) in Vancouver on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. ETHAN CAIRNS/The Canadian Press via AP

 Individual goal droughts factored into the line’s up-and-down play, too. Before his goal Friday, Lafrenière went seven games without a tally after nine in 13 games to open the year. Perreault revived his production with three goals across his last five games entering Monday. And after scoring just three times through the Rangers’ first 19 games, Zibanejad recorded his first multigoal game since March on Wednesday. 
 “I think it’s more focused on that in the beginning of the season, obviously,” Zibanejad said of his lack of scoring. “I go through a stretch like I did in the middle of the season, you don’t pay attention to it as much, maybe, but yeah, I want to score goals and I want to help the team that way, too. It’s definitely nice to see the puck go in.” 
 Zibanejad said his line has spoken about what worked best for them last year, what has clicked at times this year and what needs to happen for them to be at their best. They need to create the perfect blend of space and time with the puck — because, Zibanejad said, “we know what we’re capable of doing … when we have that time.” 
 In early October, before the Rangers home opener, head coach Mike Sullivan said the Zibanejad line hadn’t been as impactful as what they’d expected to date. They planned to give it time, to be patient. Then, he briefly separated them earlier this month, giving Pavel Dorofeyev a chance to unlock his scoring alongside Zibanejad and Lafrenière before reuniting the original line mid-game Nov. 5 before the start of their most grueling road trip of the season.

 They were on the ice for 25 scoring chances against during the West Coast trip compared to the 17 they generated, according to Natural Stat Trick, and within this Rangers structure, limiting chances remains key. Sullivan, when talking generally about the commitment to defense during this stretch of five wins in six games entering Monday, said the Blueshirts need to blend both defensive and offensive play instead of “one at the expense of the other.” 
 “When we’re at our very best, we’re a checking team that has the ability to score ,” Sullivan said, “and when we value playing defense, we can create a lot of offense through our defense, and I think we’re a lot harder to play against.” 
 And in an ideal scenario for the Rangers, a consistent top line in both areas — with Zibanejad at center, with Lafrenière and Perreault on either side — could be an anchor of that.
